title: Tensor network methods for non-perturbative dynamics of open quantum systems
authors: Thibaut Lacroix, Adam Burgess, Nicola Lorenzoni, Julian Wiercinski, Kian Damezin, James Lim, Dario Tamascelli, Alex W. Chin, Moritz Cygorek, Brendon W. Lovett, Jonathan Keeling, Susana F. Huelga, Martin B. Plenio, Erik M. Gauger
abstract: The description of open quantum system dynamics beyond the perturbative treatment (usually associated with Markovian master equations) is a computationally challenging task due to the unfavorable exponential scaling of memory kernels. Developed over recent decades in the context of quantum information and condensed matter, tensor networks provide both a new formalism and a toolbox for overcoming previous computational bottlenecks. This framework enables the formulation of non-perturbative, numerically exact methods for describing the dynamics of open quantum systems to controllable numerical accuracy. In this review, we present these methods and discuss their commonalities and differences to paint a comprehensive view of the field.
summary: This review surveys state-of-the-art methods for simulating open quantum system dynamics beyond simple approximations. It highlights that tensor networks offer a crucial, numerically exact framework to manage the exponential complexity arising from environmental memory effects. The paper provides a comprehensive guide to these advanced computational tools.
main_problem: The primary challenge is accurately simulating open quantum system dynamics when non-Markovian effects are present, as standard perturbative or Markovian approaches fail due to exponential memory kernel scaling.
main_result: Tensor networks provide a powerful and systematically improvable formalism that enables the formulation of numerically exact methods for describing these complex, non-perturbative dynamics.
method: The paper reviews various tensor network based techniques (like HEOM implementations) designed to handle the full time evolution by parameterizing quantum states efficiently, thereby overcoming exponential Hilbert space growth.
model_or_system: The focus is on open quantum systems described by a total Hamiltonian H = Hs + He + Hi, where the system S interacts with a large environment E (e.g., photonic modes or phonons).
key_observables: System reduced density matrix rho_S(t), non-Markovian memory effects.
important_parameters: Coupling strength, environmental correlation time scales, and convergence parameters for the tensor network contractions.
main_assumptions: The methods aim to be numerically exact by controlling errors through systematic parameter refinement, moving beyond uncontrolled approximations inherent in mean-field or simple perturbative treatments.
figures_summary: Figure 1 is noted as a Venn diagram classifying numerical tools based on their underlying formalism (e.g., memory kernel vs. explicit environment representation).
paper_structure: The review establishes the computational difficulty of non-Markovian OQS dynamics, contrasts Markovian/perturbative methods with the need for exact treatments, and then systematically presents tensor network approaches as the unifying, powerful toolbox.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it directly addresses advanced techniques (Tensor Networks) for simulating complex quantum systems (Open Quantum Systems) that are central to modern AMO physics and quantum optics research.

figures.caption: FIG. 1 A classification of numerical methods for open quantum system dynamics. A Venn diagram illustrating the categorization of numerical tools for open quantum system dynamics is shown. The groups are defined according to the underlying formalism of each method, such as those based on an explicit representation of the environment or on memory kernel-based approaches, which include path integral representations. Methodologies that employ a tensor network formalism, as well as those identified as numerically exact, are also indicated.

FIG. 2 Three time-step evolution of a system in the initial state ρS(0) under the influence of an environment initially in the state ρE(0). The free system evolution is given by the superoperator M = exp(LS∆t) and the red-shaded area I(α3,α′ 3)...(α0,α′ 0) encompasses the free evolution of the envi- ronment as well as its interaction with the system. The su- peroperator Jβ3 is a partial trace over the final environmental degrees of freedom. The superoperator I is the so-called pro- cess tensor of the environment; in the continuous time limit, it corresponds to the Feynman-Vernon influence functional.

FIG. 3 (a) An open system is interacting with—possibly infi- nite or continuous—environmental degrees of freedom. (b) The boundary between the ‘system’ and the environment (dashed black line) is redefined to incorporate some ‘relevant’ environmental degrees of freedom and the system of interest S within an extended system which couples to the ‘residual’ en- vironmental degrees of freedom. Under some conditions, this residual environment can be traced out to obtain a GKSL master equation for the extended system. Such a situation corresponds to a Markovian embedding of the extended sys- tem.

FIG. 4 (a) A scalar is a rank-0 tensor which is represented by a plain geometrical shape. (b) A vector is a rank-1 tensor; thus it is represented by a geometrical shape with one leg. (c) A matrix has two indices; thus its representation has two legs. (d) A rank-3 tensor is an object with 3 indices; its representation thus has three legs. (e) The trace of a n × n- matrix M is depicted by contracting the two legs of the matrix together. (f) The matrix-vector multiplication ⃗v = A⃗u, where A is a n × m-matrix and ⃗u is a m-dimensional vector and ⃗v is a n-dimensional vector.

FIG. 5 First two steps of the contraction of a pair of two- dimensional tensor networks. The red bond represents the bond under contraction. The number of indices of the result- ing yellow tensor grows rapidly after each contraction, result- ing in a computational bottleneck of two-dimensional TN.
